content: I've noticed that we us iprop(...) a lot, at least more than Rocq uses (...)%I. Has there been any attempts at reducing the number of places in which it's needed? Any insights on where the difficulty lies?
I don't have a good answer to this, but I'll note that I haven't really been trying to golf the scopes all that much.

Lean does not have a proper scoping mechanism so one needs to use something like iprop(...) to use something like scopes. In particular, in Rocq, one can associate scopes with types such that the scope is automatically opened for terms of the type. Lean does not have this mechanism. I think this is a major cause why more iprop(..) is needed in Lean than in Rocq.

@Michael Sammler what do you mean by scoping mechanism here? Lean has a way of scoping notation to a specific namespace, such that it is only available when that namespIace is opened, but I guess that's slightly different from the scoping you describe (am I right in that Rocq allows you to enable notation based on the expected type of an expression? That's pretty cool)
rocq has a concept of "locally opening a notation 'namespace' (called 'scope') in the middle of an expression", written ( expr goes here )%<scope identifier here>
and furthermore, one can attach scopes to function arguments, like "always open this scope for the third argument of function foo"
and finally, one can attach a scope to a type so that if one declares a function that takes this type as argument, that argument automatically gets this kind of scope-open behavior
I think this latter one is the one which is difficult to simulate in Lean
so this only works for "monomorphic" functions, not polymorphic ones. but then it is quite nice indeed

I think I'll join tonight's (in my timezone) #general > Office hours and ask about this. I suspect that there might not be much to do though, since Std.Do.SPred.Notation has basically the same setup as we do (they also took it from Lars' thesis), but there's no harm in asking

I'm not sure how much better it would be, but you could follow Qq's example and make the macro something really short, like i(...) and make that a scoped macro to some top-level Iris namespace that's usually expected to be opened.
there is locally scoped notation in lean as well

You could in principle put BI Props in a separate syntax category in lean, but in order to use them with the rest of "regular" lean you typically add quoting syntax to create syntactic objects in the term syntax category. In this case thought BIProps already live in the term syntax category, so iprop(...) helps disambiguate them from Prop syntax.

I think what we're really missing is the ability to open the scoped notation for a given type. Otherwise, our notation for entailment already introduces an iprop(...) for its arguments invisibly to the user, which mimicks the idea of having scopes attached to function arguments

For iprop this wouldn't be usable because in almost every situation where you use iprop, you will also use Prop. You can locally open scopes, and we already use scoped notation in cslib. So this is not the issue here.
Here's more info : https://leanprover-community.github.io/lean4-metaprogramming-book/main/05_syntax.html#typed-syntax

Shreyas Srinivas said:

For iprop this wouldn't be usable because in almost every situation where you use iprop, you will also use Prop. You can locally open scopes, and we already use scoped notation in cslib. So this is not the issue here.

What do you mean by this?

let's say you are in a section, you open a namespace within which scoped notation exists for iprop. You now have ambiguous interpretation of logical combinators. They might be combinators for iprop or for Prop. Here's a place cslib uses open scoped
Oh, I thought you meant this in the context of having iprop be a separate syntax category
From an end-user's perspective, I can't tell the difference between iprop(...) and (...)%Z

Like, I understand that your idea of using a separate syntax category for iprop would be something like this

import Lean
variable (EmptyEntails : PROP → Prop)

declare_syntax_cat iris_prop

syntax iris_prop " ⊢ " iris_prop : iris_prop
syntax "⌜" term "⌝" : iris_prop
syntax term : iris_prop
syntax "iprop(" iris_prop ")" : term
macro "⊢ " P:iris_prop : term => `(EmptyEntails iprop($P))

The issue I see with this is having that syntax term : iris_prop, which could cause issues. But maybe it's ok if we assign it a low enough priority? Or maybe it's not really an issue, because illformed expressions will be rejected when typechecking...

That kind of setup is what I was interested in exploring. Not sure if it had been tried yet, but it would allow us to define new syntax in iris_prop directly and, for instance, be able to use WP as the typeclass when in term and as a keyword for the alternate syntax when in iris_prop, which is something I now find myself wanting

Minor change

import Lean
variable (EmptyEntails : Prop → Prop)

declare_syntax_cat iris_prop

syntax iris_prop " ⊢ " iris_prop : iris_prop
syntax "⌜" term "⌝" : iris_prop
syntax "iprop(" iris_prop ")" : term
macro "⊢ " P:iris_prop : term => `(EmptyEntails iprop($P))
Wait, how is iprop currently implemented, if not via a syntax category? Is it just a single syntax listing all syntax constructions?
Why is this change needed?
Here: https://github.com/leanprover-community/iris-lean/blob/master/Iris/Iris/BI/Notation.lean

Alex Keizer said:

Wait, how is iprop currently implemented, if not via a syntax category? Is it just a single syntax listing all syntax constructions?

It is not, it's a "macro function", kinda like how the [1,2,3] notation for lists works
It quotes a term into a term

Shreyas Srinivas said:

Here: https://github.com/leanprover-community/iris-lean/blob/master/Iris/Iris/BI/Notation.lean

Also basically what Std.Do.SPred.Notation does

Here's a scoped version:

scoped version

import Lean
variable (EmptyEntails : Prop → Prop)

namespace Iris
declare_syntax_cat iris_prop

scoped syntax iris_prop " ⊢ " iris_prop : iris_prop
scoped syntax "⌜" term "⌝" : iris_prop
scoped syntax "iprop(" iris_prop ")" : term
scoped macro "⊢ " P:iris_prop : term => `(EmptyEntails iprop($P))

end Iris
But scoping this syntax doesn't really help much, in the sense that it's only useful to enable it on command, no?

Maybe it'd be useful if we had something like this?

macro "|- " P:term : term => `(Empvalid (open Iris.Notation in iprop($P))

The suggested change, making the thing inside iprop(...) a syntax category helps to control more precisely how the ... bit is parsed, and thus would serve as a different kind of scoping for custom notation than the existing namespace-based scoping for custom term notation.

You could add something like a magic wand (which is the kind of custom syntax that iprop is used for, right?) to the iris_prop syntax category entirely unscoped and it would be fine because the iris_prop category is never consulted when parsing regular terms, only when parsing the bit inside an iprop(...)

That is, I would write @Shreyas Srinivas example without scoped on the iris_prop declarations. The syntax category already scopes them in a different sense.

tweaked scoped version

import Lean
variable (EmptyEntails : Prop → Prop)

namespace Iris
declare_syntax_cat iris_prop

syntax iris_prop " ⊢ " iris_prop : iris_prop
syntax "⌜" term "⌝" : iris_prop
-- ^^ these two don't have to be scoped

scoped syntax "iprop(" iris_prop ")" : term
scoped macro "⊢ " P:iris_prop : term => `(EmptyEntails iprop($P))

end Iris

The only potential downside is you have to write your own delaborators or unexpanders. I would consider this an opportunity to format things better in the infoview. EDIT : Alex just mentioned the other downside in the message below.

But to go back to the initial question, I don't think this helps reduce the places where iprop(...) would be needed. If anything, I'd expect that making the custom syntax in a different category just enforces that iprop(...) always has to be used.

@Fernando LEAL what exactly is the problem with just using iprop(...)? Is it just that it looks ugly, or is there some other concern?

Yes, I think that the original question was more "Could we have Lean insertiprop automatically when it's expecting a term of type IProp GF? (extra credit: when it's expecting a term of type PROP where [BI PROP])". Which is something that can be done in Rocq, if I understood correctly, but not in Lean, since there's not a way to attach this to a type.

You can mimick this by adding custom notation for all functions which expect arguments in IProp which insert the iprop directly, but I dont' believe this to be scalable, and defeats the purpose of being more convenient than just wrapping things around iprop
attaching it to syntactic positions (particular arguments of particular functions) would be enough, though it could get annoying to do that manually for all iProp-taking functions

I don't think there is, no. You can only have scopes that can be opened for a definition as whole, not for specific arguments. AFAIA, the Lean way of doing so is to have a custom syntax category, and just insert the mediating macro everywhere, as we've been discussing. If there where, Qq would've been using it.

On the other hand, from experience using Qq, inserting this macro wasn't that bad of an experience (admittedly, a judgement not spoiled by having used the more powerful Rocq magic), and made slighly better by them picking a really short macro name (they use q(...)).

If iprop(...) is too bothersome, why not pick something like i(...)? Inserting 3 extra characters at a call-site is probably less hassle than adding custom notation for every function.
I don't think lean's built in syntax mechanism uses such type info when parsing syntax. It doesn't even have that info. That comes later when elaborating expressions out of the syntax.

Alex Keizer said:

If iprop(...) is too bothersome, why not pick something like i(...)? Inserting 3 extra characters at a call-site is probably less hassle than adding custom notation for every function.

Honestly, I don't thinkiprop and i make that much of a difference in the end. What I had noticed originally is that we need to use the macro itself explicitly in much more cases than in Rocq, and was wondering why. As in, what I found annoying about iprop is not having to write it, but that I seemed to need it more than usual when comparing both implementations.

What do people think about adding a notation like the following?

open Lean.Parser.Term

macro "λI" bs:funBinder* "=> " b: term : term => `(fun $bs* => iprop($b))

In the program logic a la carte port, we have the following definition, which needs to use a lot of iprop(...)

def wpiF {R} (wpi : ITree E R → (R → PROP) → PROP) :
    ITree E R → (R → PROP) → PROP :=
  λ t Φ =>
    iprop(
      |={∅}=> match t.unfold with
        | ITreeF.ret r => Φ r
        | ITreeF.tau t' => wpi t' Φ
        | ITreeF.vis i k => H.ihandle i
          (λ a => wpi (k a) Φ)
          (λ a => iprop(|={⊤,∅}=> wpi (k a) (λ _ => iprop(False))))
    )

With the notation, this would become the following, which has a lot less iprop(...) noise

def wpiF {R} (wpi : ITree E R → (R → PROP) → PROP) :
    ITree E R → (R → PROP) → PROP :=
  (λI t Φ =>
      |={∅}=> match t.unfold with
        | ITreeF.ret r => Φ r
        | ITreeF.tau t' => wpi t' Φ
        | ITreeF.vis i k => H.ihandle i
          (λ a => wpi (k a) Φ)
          (λI a => |={⊤,∅}=> wpi (k a) (λI _ => False)))

What do you think about this?

I think it's nice. I was also thinking that probably for HO resources (e.g., inv, na_inv, box and so on) we should probably also have similar wrappers. That would also make a lot of iprop(..) go away in practice.
I wish we wouldn't have to deal with iprop so much :/ But I don't see how we can do away with it just yet, so this seems like the best compromise we've got.
Could we make the |={∅}=> add the iprop(..) instead?
Also, going back to the original question I posed on this thread. What is the benefit we obtain from iprop(..)? I'm embarrased to say that's still not clear to me
λI is confusing because λx ↦ x is a valid syntax in Lean. Iλ is ok though I think.

Fernando LEAL said:

Also, going back to the original question I posed on this thread. What is the benefit we obtain from iprop(..)? I'm embarrased to say that's still not clear to me

What is your proposal for getting rid of iprop(..)? If I just remove iprop from the code above, it is not accepted by Lean. So the benefit we get is that we can write Iris formulas that are accepted by Lean.

Maybe your proposal is to just define all notations in term instead of in a special iprop syntax category? This would run into problems for notation like True, False, ∨ or ∧, which already have a meaning as terms.

Did you try checking your new fixpoint definition? When I try it, Lean complains about the iprop scope not hitting the match arms 

/--
error: elaboration function for `Iris.BI.BIBase.«term_∗_»` has not been implemented
  P ∗ Q
-/
#guard_msgs in
def match_bad (P Q : PROP) : Tag → PROP :=
  λI t => match t with
    | Tag.a => P ∗ Q
    | Tag.b => P ∧ Q

In my fixpoint definition, there is no iprop notation directly under the match arm, which is why it works in my case, but breaks in your case.

I guess ideally we would have a macro that turns

iprop(match t with
    | Tag.a => P ∗ Q
    | Tag.b => P ∧ Q)

into

match t with
    | Tag.a => iprop(P ∗ Q)
    | Tag.b => iprop(P ∧ Q)

I don't know if it is possible to write such a macro.

I should also say: The alternative to λI is to have a macro_rule that turns iprop(λ x => P) into λ x => iprop(P). Then one could write my example as the following, which would also be fine:

def wpiF {R} (wpi : ITree E R → (R → PROP) → PROP) :
    ITree E R → (R → PROP) → PROP :=
 iprop( λ t Φ =>
      |={∅}=> match t.unfold with
        | ITreeF.ret r => Φ r
        | ITreeF.tau t' => wpi t' Φ
        | ITreeF.vis i k => H.ihandle i
          (λ a => wpi (k a) Φ)
          (λ a => (|={⊤,∅}=> wpi (k a) (λ _ => (False))))
    )

I think this is nicer actually (maybe we can add some different notation so that the outer iprop doesn't need parens, and just eats the rest of the syntax in the line). Maybe you disagree, but I think having some outer marker like iprop is actually fine, it's just these inner iprops that are a nuisance.
(FWIW I think λI is an improvement too!)
I actually also like the version with only one outer iprop. The main question for me is whether one can make it work.

Cool. I think if you wanted to go ahead with either of these it would be an improvement. For posterity: I generated a little experiment here about using term elaboration (using a boolean option to disambiguate if we're elaborating an Iris term or not) but hijacking the elaboration of and/or etc. seems to be too hard.

Michael Sammler said:

I actually also like the version with only one outer iprop. The main question for me is whether one can make it work.

You totally can! Here's a proof of concept in the playground.

With that macro you can write the following:

#check iprop( λ (b : Bool) => match b with
        | true => p ∧ q
        | false => q * q
        )

which is then elaborated into a function Bool -> IProp, specifically as:

fun b =>
  match b with
  | true => p.land q
  | false => q.sand q : Bool → IProp

This is using the completely separate syntax category strategy that we talked about earlier in the thread. It's a little complex, because we now have to actually embed all the desired lean constructs into the iprop syntax category ourselves, but that embedding is exactly what then gives you the control to say that, e.g, the right-hand-side of a match should actually be parsed as an iprop rather than a term
Cool!
Let me know if this is what you guys are looking for, I'd be happy to expand the proof-of-concept into a PR that connects it with the actual IProps in Iris

One more thing I'll add: Just adding a paren-less notation for iprop which eats the rest of the term cleans up the notation a ton

def f (g : A R → (R → PROP) → PROP) :
    A R → (R → PROP) → PROP := iprop$
  fun x Φ => |={E1}=>
    match x with
    | A.a r  => Φ r
    | A.b x' => iprop$ |={E1,E2}=> g x' Φ

I made a PR with this, but feel free to close it and integrate with the other changes in the thread
Looks a lot less racket-y and a lot more lean-y (is that a word?)

We can sidestep this by using scoped notation in Lean, the issue is that we would need the scope to be open only for the arguments of bientails and other similar expression (for instance, inside of iprop(..)). I was thinking we could implement this as a macro, but does anyone know why this code doesn't work? @Alex Keizer

Playground code

class MyAdd (A : Type) where
  add : A → A → A

namespace IProp

scoped notation this " ∧ " that => MyAdd.add this that

end IProp

instance : MyAdd Nat where
  add := Nat.add

macro x:term " ⊢ " y:term : term => `(open IProp in $x > $y)
-- macro x:term " ⊢ " y:term : term => open IProp in `($x > $y) -- Also doesn't work

#eval (0 ∧ 1) ⊢ 0 -- Doesn't work...

open IProp in
#eval (0 ∧ 1) ⊢ 0 -- Does work!

Fernando LEAL said:

The issue I see with that is we would want to access the regular And anyways. But maybe we can just "wire it back" into Prop anyways

Lean allows overlapping notation, so long as the elaboration is unique (which is to say, if you have two definitions of ∧, then in every usage at least one interpretation ought to be malformed.

In playground:

axiom IProp : Type
axiom IProp.land : IProp → IProp → IProp

notation p " ∧ " q => IProp.land p q

-- works, unambigously the Prop and
variable (p q : Prop) in #check p ∧ q

-- works, unambigously the IProp and
variable (p q : IProp) in #check p ∧ q

-- error: ambigous term
variable (p q : _) in #check p ∧ q

So registering the overlapping notation will break code that relied type inference, but all such code can be fixed by adding explicit type annotations. The main loss is in the quality of error messages: what ought to be a type error might now become an ambigous notation error

I imagine we would like to hook this notation to some typeclass though, since we generalize over the type of IProp, which would always successfully elaborate and just fail to find an instance for Prop.

Tweaked example

Yeah, on second thought, it makes sense to introduce a notation typeclass (mirroring how + is driven by HAdd):

In Playground

axiom IProp : Type
axiom IProp.land : IProp → IProp → IProp

class LAnd α where
  and : α → α → α

instance instPropLAnd : LAnd Prop where
  and := And

noncomputable instance : LAnd IProp where
  and := IProp.land

notation (priority := high) p " ∧ " q => LAnd.and p q
-- ^^ high priority to completely shadow the built-in ∧ notation

-- works, unambigously the Prop and
variable (p q : Prop) in #check p ∧ q

-- works, unambigously the IProp and
variable (p q : IProp) in #check p ∧ q

-- this now works, with `p ∧ q : ?m.5`
variable (p q : _) in #check p ∧ q


-- We could make `Prop` the default instance to get some form of type inference back
attribute [default_instance] instPropLAnd

-- this now works, with `p ∧ q : Prop`
variable (p q : _) in #check p ∧ q

I have not tried this out, but I would be worried that changing ∧ to mean LAnd.and instead of And will break tactics that syntactically expect And, e.g. grind or simp. I think this can lead to extremely confusing situations where basic connectives like ∧ mean different things depending on which libraries are imported.

I had another look at function application with the syntax category, by the way, and without specifying precedences it just works: playground

/-- info: fun r => p.sand (r.sand (P (p.sand p))) : IProp → IProp -/
#guard_msgs in
#check iprop( λ r => p * r * P (p * p) )

This doesn't yet support named arguments or f ... style insertion of _s
